stem: A random variable X follows a Bernoulli distribution with parameter p = 0.6. That is, P(X=1) = 0.6 and P(X=0) = 0.4. What is the variance of X?

per_option_rationale.rationale: 0.36 = p^2 = 0.6^2; the student squares p but uses p^2 instead of p*(1-p).
0.60 is E[X] = p, not Var(X); the student reports the mean instead of the variance.
0.16 = (1-p)^2 = 0.4^2; the student squares (1-p) instead of computing p*(1-p).

explanation: For a Bernoulli(p) random variable, Var(X) = p * q where q = 1 - p. With p = 0.6 and q = 0.4: Var(X) = 0.6 * 0.4 = 0.24. Alternatively E[X^2] = p since X^2 = X for a 0/1 variable, so Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = 0.6 - 0.36 = 0.24.

explanation_sections.punchline: Bernoulli variance = pq = p(1-p), not p^2 and not p alone.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify model: Bernoulli(p) distribution. State formula: Var(X) = p(1-p). Map givens: p=0.6, q=0.4. Compute: 0.6 * 0.4 = 0.24. Cross-check: E[X]=0.6, E[X^2]=0.6 (since X^2=X for 0/1), Var=0.6-0.36=0.24.
explanation_sections.lesson: Bernoulli variance is p*q = p*(1-p); confusing it with p^2 or p is a classic error.
explanation_sections.timing: 40 seconds. One formula: Var = pq. Trap: reporting 0.6 (the mean) or 0.36 (p squared).
